title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

reading.body:
This is a false match by an automated licence plate reader, not a false claim by a model. The cameras read letters and numbers only, and Kansas can issue the same number on more than one plate design, so a plate that is not stolen can generate an alert for a stolen vehicle. The failure sits at the point where a camera alert becomes a police stop, and it is a case of a system used outside the conditions it assumes, because it treats a plate number as uniquely identifying one vehicle.

A confirmation step is meant to sit between the alert and the stop. That step worked in Colwich, where an officer recognized the minivan and found the wrong plate type had been entered, and it did not work in Catoosa, where the stop happened at gunpoint and Matthew was handcuffed before the mistake was sorted out. Catching the error inside the system rather than in the officer would have required the reader to distinguish plate backgrounds or the match to include plate type, and Kansas is moving to seven digit, nonduplicated plate numbers.

What is not established is whether the camera system or the police response was at fault in either stop, or whether any policy was breached. The account rests on one outlet's investigation and on police statements about how the alerts are meant to be confirmed.

reports.title: KAKE NEWS INVESTIGATES: Duplicate license plate numbers lead to dangerous situations for some Kansas drivers

summary:
Matthew and Leah Spurlock were repeatedly stopped because their KU Alumni license plate, number 7007, matched a stolen GMC pickup's temporary Kansas tag. In Colwich, Kansas, a Flock camera alerted police to a possible stolen vehicle, but an officer recognized their minivan and found the wrong plate type had been entered. About a month later in Catoosa, Oklahoma, another Flock camera led police to stop them at gunpoint and handcuff Matthew before the mistake was sorted out.

Kansas uses more than 100 plate designs, about half specialty, and can duplicate numbers across different plate types. Wichita police Capt. Casey Slaughter said Flock cameras read only letters and numbers, not plate backgrounds, so alerts require confirmation. He said such mistaken stops are rare. Wichita police have also talked with Flock about training its AI to recognize plate backgrounds. Kansas is moving from six digit to seven digit, nonduplicated plate numbers. The Spurlocks' stolen vehicle entry has expired, so they no longer expect stops, and they hope to keep their 7007 plate.
